questions.question: Explain the concept of inheritance in object-oriented programming
questions.answer:
Inheritance is a fundamental OOP concept where a class (derived/child class) inherits properties and methods from another class (base/parent class). This promotes code reusability and establishes a hierarchical relationship.

Key benefits include:
1. Code reusability - avoid writing duplicate code
2. Polymorphism support - enables method overriding
3. Hierarchical classification - represents real-world relationships

Types:
• Single inheritance: Child inherits from one parent
• Multiple inheritance: Child inherits from multiple parents
• Multilevel inheritance: Grandparent → Parent → Child chain
• Hybrid inheritance: Combination of multiple types

Example: A 'Vehicle' class can be inherited by 'Car' and 'Bike' classes, which inherit properties like speed, fuel, color.

questions.question: What is polymorphism? Give examples
questions.answer:
Polymorphism means 'many forms'. It allows objects to take multiple forms and methods to have multiple behaviors.

Types:
1. COMPILE-TIME POLYMORPHISM (Static):
   • Method Overloading: Same method name, different parameters
   • Operator Overloading: Same operator behaves differently

2. RUNTIME POLYMORPHISM (Dynamic):
   • Method Overriding: Child class overrides parent method
   • Achieved through virtual functions and inheritance

Example - Method Overloading:
  void print(int x) { }
  void print(String x) { }
  void print(double x) { }

Example - Method Overriding:
  Shape.draw() → Circle.draw(), Square.draw(), Triangle.draw()

questions.question: Explain encapsulation and its advantages
questions.answer:
Encapsulation is bundling data (variables) and methods (functions) into a single unit called a class, hiding internal details from outside world.

KEY PRINCIPLES:
• Data hiding: Use private/protected access modifiers
• Getter/Setter methods: Control data access
• Single Responsibility: Each class has one purpose

ADVANTAGES:
1. Security: Sensitive data is protected from unauthorized access
2. Flexibility: Implementation can change without affecting outside code
3. Maintainability: Easy to modify internal implementation
4. Read-only/Write-only properties: Control access as needed
5. Validation: Check data before assigning
6. Modularity: Each class is independent unit

Example: Bank account class keeps balance private, provides deposit() and withdraw() methods to control access.

questions.question: What is abstraction? Differentiate between abstraction and encapsulation
questions.answer:
ABSTRACTION: Showing only essential features while hiding unnecessary complexity. Uses abstract classes and interfaces to define what should be done, not how it's done.

ENCAPSULATION: Bundling data and methods into a class, controlling access using access modifiers (private, protected, public).

KEY DIFFERENCES:
┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Aspect              │ Abstraction          │ Encapsulation        │
├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Focus               │ 'What to hide'       │ 'How to hide'        │
│ Method              │ Abstract classes     │ Access modifiers     │
│                     │ Interfaces           │ Private members      │
│ Purpose             │ Reduce complexity    │ Protect data         │
│ Implementation      │ Abstract methods     │ Getter/Setter        │
│ Level               │ Design level         │ Implementation level │
│ Example             │ Abstract class Shape │ Private int balance  │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

Example: Abstract method draw() in Shape class vs private balance in BankAccount.

questions.question: What is the difference between Array and ArrayList?
questions.answer:
ARRAY vs ARRAYLIST:

ARRAY:
• Fixed size (declared at creation)
• Can store primitive types & objects
• Manual size management
• Type-safe (without generics)
• Faster access (direct index)
• Memory: Contiguous allocation
• Syntax: int[] arr = new int[5];
• Performance: Better for read-heavy operations

ARRAYLIST:
• Dynamic size (grows/shrinks automatically)
• Can only store objects (not primitives)
• Automatic size management
• Type-safe with Generics: ArrayList<Integer>
• Slightly slower (internally uses array)
• Memory: Non-contiguous, resizable
• Syntax: ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
• Performance: Better for insert/delete operations

WHEN TO USE:
• Array: Size is known and fixed, need maximum performance
• ArrayList: Size varies dynamically, need flexibility

Example:
  int[] arr = {1, 2, 3}; // Fixed size
  ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(); // Dynamic
  list.add(1);
  list.add(2);

questions.question: What are access modifiers in Java? Explain each type
questions.answer:
Access modifiers control the visibility and accessibility of classes, methods, and variables.

FOUR TYPES OF ACCESS MODIFIERS:

1. PUBLIC:
   • Most permissive
   • Accessible from anywhere (same class, package, outside package)
   • Best for API interfaces
   • Syntax: public void display() { }

2. PRIVATE:
   • Most restrictive
   • Accessible only within the same class
   • Used for sensitive data
   • Syntax: private int balance;

3. PROTECTED:
   • Accessible within same package and subclasses
   • Used in inheritance scenarios
   • Default in package, but also available in subclasses outside package
   • Syntax: protected String name;

4. DEFAULT (No modifier):
   • Accessible only within same package
   • No keyword needed
   • Package-private visibility
   • Syntax: void display() { }

COMPARISON TABLE:
┌──────────┬─────────┬─────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
│ Modifier │ Class   │ Package │ Subclass     │ Outside      │
├──────────┼─────────┼─────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
│ PUBLIC   │ ✓       │ ✓       │ ✓            │ ✓            │
│ PROTECTED│ ✓       │ ✓       │ ✓            │ ✗            │
│ DEFAULT  │ ✓       │ ✓       │ ✗            │ ✗            │
│ PRIVATE  │ ✓       │ ✗       │ ✗            │ ✗            │
└──────────┴─────────┴─────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘

questions.question: What is the difference between interface and abstract class?
questions.answer:
INTERFACE vs ABSTRACT CLASS:

INTERFACE:
• All methods are abstract (by default)
• Cannot have instance variables (only constants)
• Supports multiple inheritance
• Methods are public abstract by default
• No constructors
• Syntax: interface MyInterface { }
• Implementation: class implements Interface

ABSTRACT CLASS:
• Can have abstract and concrete methods
• Can have instance variables and state
• Supports single inheritance
• Methods can be private, protected, public
• Can have constructors
• Syntax: abstract class MyClass { }
• Implementation: class extends AbstractClass

KEY DIFFERENCES:
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│ Aspect          │ Interface        │ Abstract Class       │
├─────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Methods         │ All abstract     │ Mix of abstract      │
│                 │                  │ and concrete         │
│ Variables       │ Only constants   │ Instance variables   │
│ Inheritance     │ Multiple         │ Single               │
│ Constructor     │ Not allowed      │ Allowed              │
│ Access modifier │ Only public      │ All types            │
│ Purpose         │ Contract/spec    │ Base class concept   │
│ Keyword         │ implements       │ extends              │
└─────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

WHEN TO USE:
• Interface: Define contract, multiple inheritance needed
• Abstract Class: Share code, single inheritance, state needed

Example:
interface PaymentProcessor { void pay(); }
abstract class Animal { abstract void sound(); }

questions.question: Explain LinkedList and its advantages over ArrayList
questions.answer:
LINKEDLIST vs ARRAYLIST:

LINKEDLIST:
• Doubly linked list implementation
• Dynamic memory allocation
• Each node has data and two pointers (next, previous)
• O(1) insertion/deletion at ends
• O(n) random access
• Better for frequent insertions/deletions
• Uses more memory (extra pointers)

ARRAYLIST:
• Dynamic array implementation
• Contiguous memory allocation
• Single memory block
• O(n) insertion/deletion (shifting required)
• O(1) random access
• Better for random access
• Uses less memory

ADVANTAGES OF LINKEDLIST:
1. Efficient insertion/deletion at any position
2. No need to shift elements
3. Dynamic memory allocation
4. No capacity issues
5. Better for queue implementations

DISADVANTAGES OF LINKEDLIST:
1. Slower random access
2. Extra memory for pointers
3. Cache unfriendly (non-contiguous)
4. More complex implementation

COMPARISON:
┌─────────────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐
│ Operation           │ ArrayList   │ LinkedList   │
├─────────────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
│ Random access       │ O(1)        │ O(n)         │
│ Insert at start     │ O(n)        │ O(1)         │
│ Insert at end       │ O(1)        │ O(1)         │
│ Insert at middle    │ O(n)        │ O(n)         │
│ Delete at start     │ O(n)        │ O(1)         │
│ Delete at end       │ O(1)        │ O(1)         │
│ Memory overhead     │ Low         │ High         │
└─────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘

questions.question: What is a String? Why are Strings immutable in Java?
questions.answer:
STRING IN JAVA:

A String is a sequence of characters stored as an object. It's immutable, meaning once created, its value cannot be changed.

WHY STRINGS ARE IMMUTABLE:

1. SECURITY:
   • String is used for authentication (passwords, usernames)
   • If strings were mutable, hackers could change values
   • Database connections use strings - must be secure

2. THREAD SAFETY:
   • Immutable objects are thread-safe by nature
   • No synchronization needed
   • Multiple threads can safely use same string

3. HASHMAP EFFICIENCY:
   • Strings used as HashMap keys
   • If value changes, hash code changes
   • Immutability ensures consistent hash code

4. CACHING:
   • JVM caches strings in string pool
   • If mutable, cache would be corrupted
   • Saves memory through string interning

5. CLASSLOADER:
   • Strings used in class loading
   • Immutability prevents code injection

STRING VS STRINGBUILDER VS STRINGBUFFER:

STRING:
• Immutable
• Thread-safe
• Slower for modifications
• For fixed content

STRINGBUILDER:
• Mutable
• Not thread-safe
• Faster for modifications
• Single-threaded scenarios

STRINGBUFFER:
• Mutable
• Thread-safe (synchronized)
• Slower than StringBuilder
• Multi-threaded scenarios

Example:
String s = "Hello"; // Immutable
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello");
sb.append(" World"); // Efficient modification
